A1.justification: Despite the changed title, both PDFs describe the same SSA research, with matching methods, synthetic tasks, and retained figures. All 15 pages of v1 and 14 pages of v2, including appendices and image-based prompts, support reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original quantifier and linear-function experiments, architectural ablations, LLaMA evaluations, GPT-2 language-modeling results, and BabyBERTa probing results.

after.justification: V2 retains original synthetic-task and BabyBERTa results and reports additional temperature-scaled Softmax comparisons and downstream NLP benchmark outcomes.

M1.justification: Both versions use the same normalized SSA scoring formula in Equation (5), with unchanged model architecture and losses. V1 already permits fixed or learned exponents. V2 changes which variants are evaluated and expands the explanation, without establishing a new SSA training or inference procedure.

E1.justification: Decoder training and perplexity evaluation change from OpenWebText to FineWebText; the separate OpenWebText token-norm analysis remains. V2 adds ARC-Challenge, ARC-Easy, HellaSwag, LAMBADA, and seven SuperGLUE tasks. Reported BabyBERTa coverage contracts from 17 to 12 probes. The synthetic quantifier and affine-function tasks remain.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds temperature-scaled Softmax comparators at T = 5, 10, 20, 50, and 100. Standard Softmax, SOFT/AVG, the four-scoring-function mixture, CosFormer, SA-Softmax, and LLaMA 3.3 70B remain in that comparison.

E3.justification: The reported GPT-2 training budget changes from 20,000 to 50,000 steps. V2 consistently specifies 124M parameters, whereas v1's experimental section says 134M but other passages say 124M. V2 adds zero-shot and three-shot benchmark accuracy, drops holistic BabyBERTa evaluation and some SSA configurations, and replaces the linear-function prompt's decimal demonstrations with integer examples explicitly specifying f(x) = ax + b. These reported changes do not establish that retained LLaMA results were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds a temperature-sensitivity investigation asking whether softening Softmax remedies linear-function generalization failures. Exponent exploration narrows through removal of trainable-exponent GPT-2 results and BabyBERTa SSA-1.1. Existing architectural ablations, distribution-shift analyses, boundary-value examples, and hybrid-scoring experiments remain, with the latter discussion moved to Appendix B.

E5.justification: The shared seed for generating 100 linear test functions remains in v1 Appendix J and v2 Appendix K, as do the synthetic evaluation averaging procedures. Neither version reports repeated-training-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests; the new benchmark tables also contain point estimates.

E6.justification: V2 adds temperature-comparison scores and substantial downstream benchmark results, including zero-shot ARC-Challenge accuracy of 20.8% for Softmax versus 23.2% for SSA. V1's decoder loss and trainable-SSA results, numerous BabyBERTa entries, and overall probe averages disappear. Retained synthetic and BabyBERTa values match. GPT-2 perplexities are now reported under changed corpus and training conditions, so they do not establish a same-setting improvement over v1.

T1.justification: Section 7 changes the stated exponent domain from n > 1 to n >= 1 and explicitly discusses the b = n = 1 linear endpoint. However, the definition accompanying Equation (5) still requires n > 1. The scoring formula and existing saturation and exponential-limit reasoning otherwise remain; no new theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The title, abstract, and introduction broaden the principal NLP contribution from language modeling and grammatical probing to superiority on standard zero-shot and few-shot early-learning benchmarks. The conclusion additionally claims improved generalization without losing accuracy. The central claim that SSA mitigates Softmax-related ICL limitations remains.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly interprets failures across model sizes as architectural limitations, acknowledges that some tasks benefit from concentrated attention, and adds task-specific interpretations of BabyBERTa gains and potential applicability to large-scale language modeling. V1's explanation involving nearly constant Softmax scores for small inputs is removed. The main limitations concerning model scale and simultaneous input/function distribution shifts remain.

D1.justification: V2 identifies the LM Eval harness and adds A100 80GB hardware and approximately 120 GPU-hours per GPT-2 model, exceeding 240 GPU-hours combined. It also revises the disclosed linear-function prompt. The SSA code link, Adam learning rate, and LLaMA LoRA training details remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Related work adds attention-concentration and token-dominance research by Tian, Vig, Htut, Sekhsaria, and Mamidanna, while removing the dedicated induction-head paragraph. New corpus, benchmark, and evaluation-harness references are added; Salazar and Zaczynska are removed. The broader ICL lineage and positioning of SSA as a Softmax alternative remain.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, SSA motivation, NLP discussion, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Hybrid-scoring discussion moves from Section 6 to Appendix B, ICL effects receive subsection 7.1, and the former standalone NLP section becomes subsection 7.2. These changes substantially reorganize the narrative beyond adding experiments.

P2.justification: V2 expands Table 1, adds a downstream benchmark table, and converts the wide BabyBERTa table into a reduced single-column table. Three prompt screenshots become readable boxed text. Existing plots are retained but resized or relocated, and appendix material is substantially repacked. This materially changes the presentation of evidence.

improvement.justification: The added temperature controls and downstream benchmarks strengthen empirical breadth, while clearer prompts and compute disclosure improve documentation. However, all five omitted BabyBERTa probes favor Softmax over both retained SSA variants. V2 also removes holistic results and overall MLM averages, which showed SSA-2 below Softmax, 72.48 versus 73.01, without explaining the selection. These omissions weaken balanced assessment of SSA's benefits and failures. The gains and losses provide no reliably assessable net direction for overall paper quality.
